plain: Hugging Face is a public warehouse where thousands of companies and universities leave their AI models for anyone to take. Think of it as a huge public library: you walk in for free, you see every shelf, and each book has a label stuck on it saying what you're allowed to do with it. Some you can photocopy and sell; others you can only read at home. Each model is a large file that has already learned to do one specific thing: transcribe audio, translate, write text, describe a photo. The expensive part is never the file — it's not having read the label before building a business on top of it.

account.free: Yes, and the free tier is more than enough for this whole course: unlimited downloads of public models, uploading your own, and running demos on a basic machine. The PRO account costs about $9 a month and gives you faster machines for demos and some credit for trying models without installing them; you don't need it to learn. The enterprise plan starts around $20 per person per month. Downloading models doesn't cost money, but it does cost gigabytes on your disk: a medium-sized one takes up 14 GB.
steps: Go to huggingface.co. At the top right there are two links: 'Log In' and 'Sign Up'. Click 'Sign Up'. It just asks for email and password.

The second screen asks for 'Username'. Careful: it's public and effectively permanent, it shows up in front of everything you upload, in the form 'levi/my-model'. Pick something professional, not a nickname. 'Full name' and 'Homepage' are optional, leave them blank if you want.
You'll get a message with a link. Until you click it you can't download gated models or upload anything. Check your spam folder, it often lands there.
In the top menu click 'Models'. You'll see a list sorted by 'Trending' (what's popular this week) and, on the left, a column of filters. 90% of what you'll do here lives there.
Filter by task and by license

In the left column, 'Tasks' groups models by what they're for: 'Text Generation' is writing text, 'Automatic Speech Recognition' is turning audio into text, 'Text-to-Image' is generating images. Further down, under 'Licenses', check 'apache-2.0' or 'mit'. With that, you'll only see models you can bill for.
Read the model card before downloading

Open any model. The 'Model card' tab is the product label: below the name there's a row of gray tags, and one of them starts with 'License:'. That word decides whether you can invoice with this model or not. The 'Files and versions' tab tells you how much it actually weighs.
Create an access token only when you need one

At the top right, on your profile picture: 'Settings' → 'Access Tokens' → 'Create new token'. It's a long password used to download from your computer. It's shown only once: if you close the window without copying it, there's no way to recover it, you have to delete it and create another. Never paste it in an email or a chat.
account.warning: Being able to download a model doesn't mean you can sell it. Licenses that allow charging and licenses that explicitly forbid it coexist here, and that small label on the card is a contract you accept the moment you use the file. Second warning: some models, like Meta's or Google's, show you a form and an 'Agree and access repository' button. Clicking it sends your name, email, and country to that company. That can't be undone.

first: Type 'whisper' in the search bar at the top and open 'openai/whisper-large-v3'. It's the model that converts speech to text and is used by half the world.
Look at the row of gray tags under the name and find 'License: apache-2.0'. Apache 2.0 means: use it, sell it, you owe me nothing.
Look at the two counters on the right: downloads last month and hearts. Millions of downloads means that, if something breaks, a thousand people have already written about it online.
Go into 'Files and versions' and find the file ending in '.safetensors'. You'll see it weighs about 3 GB. That's the actual model; the rest are notes and configuration.

Go back to 'Models', filter 'Tasks' = 'Automatic Speech Recognition' and 'Licenses' = 'apache-2.0', and see how many alternatives come up. That reflex, filtering by license before falling in love with a model, is what will save you the heartbreak.
words: A file that has already learned to do something and whose owner has published it for you to download to your own computer. The opposite is a closed model, which lives on someone else's server and you can only use it by paying every time you call it.

What's inside that file: millions of numbers that are, literally, what the machine learned while it was being trained. When someone says 'the weights have been released', it means you can now have it on your own disk.

The presentation page written by whoever published it: what it's for, what data it was trained on, what it does badly, and what permission it grants you. It's the first thing to read and the thing most people skip.

The way size is measured. When you see '7B' it means seven billion of those internal numbers. It's used to work out whether it'll fit: as a rule of thumb, a 7B model needs about 14 GB of memory to run.
The owner doesn't hand out the file blindly: first they ask you to say who you are and accept their terms. It's not the same as forbidden; it's a front desk with a sign-in book.
The most convenient permission. Apache 2.0 and MIT are the two names you'll see: they let you put the model inside a product you charge for, with no permission needed and nothing owed to anyone.

The permission that cuts you off. If the tag carries the letters 'NC' or says 'research only', you can play, study, and teach, but the moment someone pays you for something that uses that model, you're in breach.
matters: Check the license before building, not after. Spending three months of work on top of a model tagged 'cc-by-nc-4.0' and discovering it once you already have paying customers leaves you two options, both bad: rebuild it from scratch or shut it down.

Open doesn't mean unconditional. Llama, from Meta, does let you charge, but it forces you to visibly write 'Built with Llama' in your product. Gemma, from Google, also allows commercial use, but keeps a list of prohibited uses that binds you. You either comply or you don't use it.

Size decides your bill, not quality. A 70B model doesn't fit on a normal laptop: either you rent a machine with a powerful graphics card, which runs about $1 an hour, or you choose a 7B one. Going with the giant 'because it's better' is the fastest way to spend $300 in a month of testing.

The date and download counter warn you about abandonment. A model with 40 downloads and a last update from three years ago has no community behind it: when you hit an error, no one will have already solved it, and you're on your own in front of a file you don't understand.
ignore: The 'Spaces', which are demos people set up to show their model working. They're fine and will come in handy someday, but they don't help you decide which model to use.
The block of code that almost every card has halfway down the page. That's for people who already code. Right now you're learning to choose, which is the part that doesn't get automated.

The results tables with acronyms like MMLU, ARC, or HellaSwag. They're scores from multiple-choice-style tests run on the models, and one can score better than another and still serve you worse for your specific case.

questions.prompt: You find a model that transcribes Spanish audio better than anything you've tried. On its card, the tag reads 'License: cc-by-nc-4.0'. Your plan was to put it into a tool you're going to charge $29 a month for.

options.text: Discard it and look for another one that does the same thing with an Apache 2.0 or MIT license, filtering by license in the left-hand column.
options.why: Those two letters, NC, mean 'non-commercial', and there's no button or payment that removes them: you'd need a private agreement with the author and a lawyer. Also, for audio transcription you have plenty of alternatives with a permissive license, starting with Whisper, so switching costs you an afternoon, not a lawsuit.

options.text: Use it anyway: it's published openly, anyone can download it, and it didn't even ask for a password.
options.why: It's what almost everyone thinks the first time, because downloading is so easy that nothing feels like it's been signed. It breaks the day you invoice: by using the weights you accept the license, and that license forbids exactly what you're doing. Nobody watching doesn't change what you agreed to.

options.text: Use it but credit the author clearly on the website and in the app's footer.
options.why: It's half logical, and that's what makes it deceptive: the 'BY' part of that license really is satisfied by crediting the author. But there are two conditions there and you're only meeting one. The 'NC' isn't offset by credit or links, because it's not a request for recognition, it's a ban on charging money.

questions.explain: Being able to download it isn't the same as being able to sell it: the label rules over the button.

questions.prompt: You want to try Llama 3.1 8B. You go to its page and there's no download button: there's a form with your name and country, a checkbox, and a button that says 'Agree and access repository'.

options.text: Read the terms and, if you accept them, go ahead knowing you're sending your data to Meta and that you're bound to put 'Built with Llama' on the product you build.
options.why: That form isn't a decorative formality, it's the exact moment you sign. You accept with your eyes open: you know what data leaves here, you know it can't be undone, and you know exactly what obligation stays attached to your product. That's exactly what's expected of someone who charges for doing this.

options.text: Look for the same model on another user's account who re-uploaded it without the restriction and download it from there, since it downloads just as well.
options.why: Those copies really do exist and work, which is why a lot of people go that route and feel fine about it. The flaw is glaring: the license travels with the model, not with the page you download it from. You saved yourself a form and ended up with nothing to show the day a client, or their legal department, asks where this came from.

options.text: Interpret that, if they're asking you to identify yourself, the model can't be used commercially, and look for another one.
options.why: It's the cautious reaction, and that's why so many people rule out Llama without ever reading it. But you're mixing up two different things: gated means 'I want to know who's taking it', non-commercial means 'don't charge with this'. Llama does allow charging, with conditions. By conflating them you rule out one of the most useful model families out there, over a fear that didn't apply.

questions.explain: Gated means they want your name and details, not that you can't use it.
